from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Core Strategy: Exploiting Symmetry", [
            "Exploit symmetry to simplify complex systems.",
            "Symmetry reduces search space for solutions.",
            "Check centroids when systems show rotational symmetry.",
            "Set variables equal to solve algebraic complexity.",
            "Symmetry is a powerful reduction technique."
        ])
        
        shape = RegularPolygon(n=6, color=WHITE).scale(1.0)
        self.place_at_grid(shape, 'C3')
        self.add(shape)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.play(FadeIn(shape))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        self.play(Rotate(shape, angle=90 * DEGREES))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FF0000"))
        axis = Line(start=UP*2, end=DOWN*2, color=RED).move_to(shape.get_center())
        self.play(Create(axis))
        self.play(shape.animate.flip(axis=RIGHT))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.play(FadeOut(axis), shape.animate.rotate(-90 * DEGREES).flip(axis=RIGHT))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        self.play(shape.animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Pigeonhole Principle & Extremal Method", [
            "Combine invariants with the Extremal Principle.",
            "Focus on the largest or smallest element.",
            "Extremal values create contradictions or base cases."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFF00")
        
        holes = VGroup(*[Circle(radius=0.3, color=WHITE) for _ in range(5)])
        holes.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.2)
        self.place_at_grid(holes, 'C2')
        self.add(holes)
        
        pigeons = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.15, color="#FF0000") for _ in range(6)])
        for p in pigeons:
            p.move_to(np.array([-3, 2, 0]))
        self.add(pigeons)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")
        
        animations = []
        for i in range(5):
            animations.append(pigeons[i].animate.move_to(holes[i].get_center()))
        animations.append(pigeons[5].animate.move_to(holes[0].get_center() + UP * 0.6))
        self.play(*animations, run_time=2)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFF00")
        
        pigeons[5].set_color("#00FF00")
        self.play(Indicate(pigeons[5]), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(1)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):

        lecture_lines = [
            "Analyze symmetry to unlock the problem.",
            "Identify invariants to track system state.",
            "Apply the extremal principle to conclude."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Conclusion: Developing Your Toolkit", lecture_lines)
        
        # Create Key icons for the toolbox
        key_colors = [BLUE_B, GREEN_B, YELLOW_B]

        self.play(FadeIn(keys[0]))

        self.play(FadeIn(keys[1]))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW_B))
        self.place_at_grid(keys[2], 'D2')
        self.play(FadeIn(keys[2]))

        extra_text = Text("Practice Makes Perfect", font_size=32, color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(extra_text, 'E4')

outline.topic: Mastering Putnam Competition Problem-Solving: The Art of Symmetry and Invariants
outline.target_audience: University students with a strong background in competition mathematics

sections.title: Introduction: The Putnam Mindset (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Define the Putnam mindset: moving beyond textbook formulas to creative, first-principle thinking. Introduce the concept of 'Invariants'—properties that remain unchanged despite a system's evolution.
sections.example: Visualize a robotic chameleon on a checkerboard. No matter how many times it jumps, the color of the square it sits on follows a parity invariant.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Discrete vs. Continuous Invariants (0:45-1:45)
sections.content: Before solving complex problems, categorize tools: parity (odd/even), modular arithmetic (discrete), and monotone functions or potentials (continuous). Use animated flowcharts to show how these tools narrow down search spaces.
sections.example: A graph showing an 'Energy Level' decreasing until it hits a stable minimum (a common technique for Putnam optimization problems).

sections.title: Core Strategy: Exploiting Symmetry (1:45-3:15)
sections.content: Introduce symmetry as a reduction technique. If an expression or geometric configuration is invariant under permutation, the solution often lies on the line of symmetry or at the centroid.
sections.example: A rotating hexagon with numbers at its vertices. If the system is rotationally symmetric, we can set all variables equal to simplify the algebraic complexity instantly.

sections.title: Application: The Pigeonhole Principle & Extremal Method (3:15-4:30)
sections.content: Combine invariants with the Extremal Principle—always consider the 'largest' or 'smallest' element in a set to create a contradiction or a base case for induction.
sections.example: A fox chasing a rabbit in a grid. By considering the 'minimal distance' to a corner as an invariant/monotone value, we prove whether the rabbit can ever be caught.

sections.title: Conclusion: Developing Your Toolkit (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize the cycle: Analyze symmetry -> Identify an invariant -> Apply the extremal principle. Encourage viewing problems as interactive systems rather than static equations.
sections.example: A recap graphic displaying the three key tools as 'keys' unlocking a locked puzzle box.
